title: A clump population framework for star formation across galactic scales
abstract: Whether star formation across different spatial scales and galactic environments follows universal laws remains poorly understood. We investigate cloud-scale star formation in 30 dwarf and disk galaxies. Molecular clouds are identified using a dendrogram algorithm, and their molecular gas masses ($M_{\rm H_2}$) and star formation rates (SFRs) are derived from integrated CO and mid-infrared emission, respectively. We find a consistent $M_{\rm H_2}$--SFR relation across all galaxies, with little sensitivity to galactic environment. Extending the analysis to Milky Way cloud substructures down to sub-parsec scales and 311 diverse nearby galaxies, we find that this relation persists across ten orders of magnitude in molecular gas mass and SFR. A theoretical model in which star formation occurs within dense clumps embedded in molecular clouds reproduces this observed relation. The weak environmental dependence of star formation at the clump scale provides a possible explanation for the nearly universal $M_{\rm H_2}$--SFR relation across galaxies. This framework establishes an observationally grounded connection between star formation in the Milky Way and external galaxies.

title: A ${}^{13}$CO Detection in a Massive Molecular Gas Flow in Abell 1795's Central Galaxy
abstract: We present new ALMA ${}^{13}$CO(2-1) observations of the central galaxy in the cool-core cluster Abell 1795, targeting the origin of extended molecular filaments. The filaments extend for 5--7 kpc and are closely drawn up around large radio bubbles inflated by jets from the central active galactic nucleus (AGN). Smooth velocity gradients along their lengths are consistent with entrained flows lifted by the expanding bubbles. Here we detect the northern molecular filament in the low-opacity molecular tracer ${}^{13}$CO(2-1), which can provide a more reliable measure of the molecular gas mass and conditions than ${}^{12}$CO. The velocity structure in ${}^{13}$CO(2-1) is consistent with that of the ${}^{12}$CO(2-1) emission. Using a range of plausible excitation temperatures and covering fractions, we thereby determine a filament molecular gas mass of (0.1--2) $\times \ 10^9 \ \text{M}_\odot$, or down to an order of magnitude below previous estimates. This implies a CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor of $α_\text{CO} =$ 0.4--5 $\ \text{M}_\odot $ (K km s$^{-1}$ pc$^2)^{-1}$ in the filament, or $\sim$ 0.1--1 times the standard assumption of the Milky Way value. Direct entrainment by the N radio bubble is now plausible, as it can provide sufficient mechanical energy and buoyant support for the molecular gas flow. Similarly, measured X-ray cooling rates are also now consistent with in-situ condensation of uplifted, low-entropy hot gas. Both formation mechanisms require multiple generations of bubbles at higher filament masses.

title: Direct measures of black hole masses through cosmic time
abstract: Supermassive black holes (BHs) are thought to reside in all massive galaxies. They play a fundamental role in shaping galaxy evolution by suppressing star formation and halting the stellar growth of the most massive galaxies via feedback mechanisms. However, to date, measuring even their most basic property, their mass, is still challenging. The mass of BHs carries information on the growth history and the mutual interplay with the host galaxy. Uncertain BH masses leave many key questions on galaxy evolution wide open. Here we show that a transformational facility such as ALMA2040 would open a new window to measure BH mass by directly observing the kinematics of cold gas in galaxy cores from the local Universe up to very high redshift, irrespective of BH activity. This would revolutionise our understanding of BH formation, growth, and their role within galaxy evolution.

title: Probing cold gas and dust in quiescent galaxies across cosmic time
abstract: The discovery of massive quiescent galaxies at high redshift by JWST has revealed that star formation can cease rapidly in the early Universe, yet the physical mechanisms responsible for quenching remain unknown. A key missing element is the systematic measurement in statistically representative quiescent samples of the cold gas and dust content, which are crucial for distinguishing quenching mechanisms and evolutionary pathways. Such observations are currently not feasible because state-of-the-art sub-millimeter facilities (e.g., ALMA) cannot routinely detect the faint molecular gas and dust reservoirs of quiescent galaxies, nor pinpoint outflowing molecular gas. A next-generation facility (ALMA2040) capable of providing transformative access to the cold interstellar medium of quiescent galaxies across redshift is therefore essential. In particular, it will allow the community to probe the molecular gas content of quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon and beyond by targeting the CO, [CI], and [CII] emission lines, as well as unveiling the physical conditions of the cold interstellar medium by constraining the CO spectral line energy distribution. It will also reveal the dust content of the passive population, a crucial ingredient to constrain the different quenching mechanisms. Finally, it will enable probing the molecular gas kinematics and identify molecular outflows driven by supermassive black holes. When combined with the rich legacy of JWST, ELT, and SKAO surveys, ALMA2040 will deliver a comprehensive, multi-phase view of feedback and quenching, allowing us to establish when, how, and why galaxies shut down their star formation across cosmic time.

title: Dust at cosmic dawn: unveiling the onset of dust and obscured star formation at $z\gtrsim8$
abstract: Although less than 1 percent of the baryonic mass budget of a galaxy, cosmic dust profoundly alters the multi-wavelength appearance of galaxies across cosmic time. The (sub)millimeter wavelength regime is uniquely capable of weighing these dust reservoirs, and revealing the total extent of galaxy evolution that remains hidden behind them. With current facilities, however, doing so at $z > 8$ is largely out of reach. ALMA2040, a next-generation (sub)millimeter interferometer, is set to change this. Through an order-of-magnitude increase in sensitivity compared to ALMA, ALMA2040 is a transformational facility that will be able to routinely detect dust emission from galaxies at $z > 8$ and, through simultaneous multi-band characterization, accurately measure their dust masses, temperatures, and infrared luminosities. Combined with ancillary metallicity measurements -- including from the far-infrared lines detected by ALMA2040 itself -- this will establish the relative roles of supernovae and grain growth in building up dust in the earliest galaxies. Simultaneously, ALMA2040 will measure the fraction of star formation that is obscured by dust at cosmic dawn, and thereby the extent to which rest-UV and optical surveys miss early galaxy build-up. Without a 10$\times$ upgrade to ALMA -- comparable to the leap from the VLT to the ELT -- we will not be able to capitalize on the momentous advances enabled by JWST, and will remain blind to the cold and obscured component of galaxy formation in the $z > 8$ Universe.

title: Resolving the Assembly of Disk Galaxies from the Epoch of Reionisation to Cosmic Noon
abstract: Most of the mass and angular momentum of today's disk galaxies assembled at $z>1$. Yet, it remains unclear how these galaxies acquired their gas, how their baryons and dark matter coevolved, and how feedback and radial gas transport shaped their disks. Addressing these gaps requires resolved observations of cold gas, which carries most of the mass and angular momentum involved in galaxy assembly. By resolving CO and [C II] at kpc scales, ALMA revealed a surprising population of rotation-dominated disks, even at $z>2$, exhibiting kinematic signatures consistent with spiral arms, bars, and tidal tails. Yet, these studies are limited to massive ($M_\star>10^{10.5}$ M$_\odot$) and highly star-forming (SFRs$\gtrsim 100$ M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$) galaxies, the progenitors of today's most massive elliptical and disk galaxies. To understand how most present-day spirals (like the Milky Way) assembled, it is crucial to resolve their low-mass progenitors, which dominate the star-forming galaxy population by number at $z>1$. Achieving this goal demands a tenfold increase in line sensitivity and hence a next-generation sub-/millimetre facility: ALMA2040. This leap in sensitivity will enable routine resolved studies of hundreds of $M_\star>10^9$ M$_\odot$ galaxies, including those on and below the main sequence of star-forming galaxies, providing representative, statistical galaxy samples with sub-kpc constraints on the cold gas kinematics and morphology. By uniquely providing resolved CO, [C I], and [C II] observations across $z=1-6$, ALMA2040 will trace a much larger fraction of the cold-gas reservoir than is accessible today, extending resolved studies from rare massive and/or lensed systems to representative galaxy populations. In this way, ALMA2040 will transform our understanding of how galaxy disks formed and evolved.

title: Unveiling star formation at sub-solar metallicity with ALMA2040
abstract: A fundamental question in astrophysics is whether the processes governing star formation are universal or depend on the physical conditions of their local galactic environment. The Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds offer ideal laboratories to explore this question, as the gas conditions in them span up to orders of magnitude in metallicity, gas surface density, ambient pressure, dust abundance, radiation field, and cosmic-ray flux. In particular, both the outer Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds provide the closest low-metallicity environments with conditions similar to those of metal-poor galaxies, while remaining sufficiently close to soon allow spatial resolution of individual star-forming cores and disks. Recent observations with ALMA and other facilities have begun to unveil the physical and chemical properties of star-forming regions in low-metallicity environments. Yet, their distances from the Sun still require transformational gains in current ALMA capabilities to address fundamental open questions: (1) Are the properties of prestellar cores universal? (2) Does cloud fragmentation, and the resulting stellar IMF, depend critically on metallicity? (3) How does dust evolution depend on metallicity, and what is the impact in the survival of protoplanetary disks? (4) Is the reduced amount of metals and dust shielding at low metallicity critical for the formation and survival of molecules? ALMA2040 will identify similarities and differences between solar- and sub-solar-metallicity star-forming regions, and answer the question: how do different environmental conditions influence the physical and chemical pathways leading to star formation?

title: Are High-EW LAEs good analogs for the earliest galaxies? A study on the ionizing conditions and gas properties of LAEs at $2\lesssim z\lesssim7
abstract: Lyman-$α$ emitters (LAEs) are frequently proposed as analogs of the low-mass, metal-poor galaxies thought to dominate cosmic reionization. In particular, galaxies with large Ly$α$ equivalent widths (EWs) are expected to have not experienced significant chemical enrichment. We test this hypothesis using a sample of 88 LAEs at $2 \lesssim z\lesssim 7$, selected from MUSE observations that are undetected in deep HST imaging and subsequently followed up with JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy. Despite the unprecedented sensitivity of JWST, only 50 of the LAEs exhibit secure counterparts in available deep NIRCam imaging reaching typical 3$σ$ depths of $m_\text{AB}\sim30.3$ mag, highlighting the intrinsically faint nature of the population. Gas-phase metallicities are inferred by fitting optical emission lines with a grid of BPASS+cloudy photoionization models, while stellar masses are derived from NIRCam photometry through SED fitting. The final sample with secure stellar masses and gas-phase metallicities encompasses only 16 LAEs, occupying regions of standard emission-line diagnostic diagrams consistent with low-metallicity star-forming systems. Although the strong-line metallicity diagnostic R3 appears to decrease with increasing EW, we find no compelling evidence for a strong monotonic relation between EW and gas-phase metallicity when metallicities are inferred through full emission-line fitting. However, galaxies with stronger Ly$α$ emission tend to lie below the average mass-metallicity relation at fixed stellar masses, suggesting that they are preferentially less chemically evolved than typical galaxies of the same mass. We conclude that high-EW LAEs provide useful, though imperfect, analogs of the galaxies thought to drive cosmic reionization, and combining EW with stellar mass may provide a more effective route for identifying the most chemically primitive galaxies.

title: Disk tilts in Milky Way-like galaxies and their link to mergers
abstract: We investigated disk reorientation and its relationship to mergers in a sample of 93 Milky Way-mass galaxies drawn from the TNG50 simulations. From this sample, we identified 117 individual disk-tilt events with clearly defined start and end times, and we divided them into two classes based on whether the disk evolves smoothly or undergoes rapid disruption and regrowth during the tilt duration. For each tilt event, we linked the most massive merger that occurs in close temporal association with it. We focus on those tilt events occurring during phases of smooth disk evolution, which typically show tilt rates below 10 degrees per Gyr, persist for 2-9 Gyr, and are generally connected to minor mergers. Roughly 40% of these events reach tilt angles exceeding 30 degrees, most often triggered by satellites whose masses are comparable to or less massive than the galaxy's total stellar mass, merging on tangential orbits with orbital angular momentum that is retrograde or nearly perpendicular to the disk spin. The satellite consistently drives the disk tilt toward alignment with the satellite's orbital spin; satellites that came in on retrograde orbits relative to the disk spin can thus induce large tilt angles and can produce an almost orthogonal configuration between the stellar disk and the satellite's orbital plane as an intermediate phase. Owing to the comparatively slow tilt rates, the stellar disk can keep stable and continue to grow throughout the reorientation process. Consequently, galaxies that experience strong disk tilts can still maintain stellar disks that are as thin as those in systems without significant reorientation.

title: The Birth and Early Feedback of Massive Star Clusters Across the Local Universe
abstract: Young massive star clusters (YMCs; ${\gtrsim}10^4\rm\,M_\odot$) represent a distinct, extreme mode of star formation and the closest present-day analogues of the environments in which globular clusters and Cosmic Noon stellar populations assembled. Given the extreme dust extinction in the earliest phase of YMC formation, (sub-)millimeter observations are the only means of probing their assembly and early feedback. Pioneering works with ALMA are limited to individual region studies and to the most massive YMCs in them, leaving many open questions about the initial conditions of YMC formation, the integrated star and cluster formation efficiencies, the dominant pre-supernova feedback channels, and the prevalence and reach of cluster-driven outflows. ALMA2040 will enable mass-complete, resolved surveys in hundreds of host galaxies, transforming the study of massive cluster formation and feedback from individual case analyses into statistical measurements across the full range of galactic environments.

title: Dust Activity Evolution and Constraints on Icy Grains in the Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
abstract: We present Zwicky Transient Facility observations of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS to characterize its dust-activity evolution before and after perihelion. Before perihelion, the effective scattering cross section $C_{\rm e}$ brightened across the inner $2\times10^4$ km as $C_{\rm e}\propto r_{\rm H}^{-γ}$, with $γ$ increasing from $1.63\pm0.14$ to $1.88\pm0.34$ with aperture size. After perihelion, the heliocentric index decreased from $2.44\pm0.09$ in the $5\times10^3$ km aperture to $1.54\pm0.09$ in the $8\times10^4$ km aperture, indicating faster fading of the inner coma. Under adopted grain-size and residence-time assumptions, the implied dust mass-loss rates are $\sim123$--$203~{\rm kg~s^{-1}}$ before perihelion and $\sim596$--$1412~{\rm kg~s^{-1}}$ after perihelion. The morphology yields a sunward ejection-speed scale of $v_{\rm ej}\sim(190\pm3)a_{μ{\rm m}}^{-1/2}~{\rm m~s^{-1}}$ and an effective perpendicular velocity of $v_\perp=(79\pm6)a_{μ{\rm m}}^{-1/2}~{\rm m~s^{-1}}$. Post-perihelion surface-brightness profiles transiently steepened to $k\sim-2.7$ in late November and early December, then became shallower and approached $k=-1.5$ by January. Matched $g-r$ profiles show that this phase coincided with an anomalously blue outer coma that disappeared by January. We characterize the fading component with a projected destruction length of $\ell_{\rm DE}\sim(6.4$--$7.2)\times10^4$ km. Thermophysical sublimation calculations indicate that this scale, together with the order of magnitude of the water production near the main imaging epoch, is consistent with $a_0\sim5$--$10~μ{\rm m}$ icy grains containing a small absorbing carbonaceous fraction of $f_{\rm C}\sim0.1\%$. These results suggest that the early post-perihelion coma likely contained a short-lived, volatile-bearing icy-grain component whose fading contributed to the outer-coma brightness and color evolution

title: A machine-learning-driven dataset of 144,111 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon infrared spectra for interpreting aromatic infrared bands
abstract: The interpretation of interstellar aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) relies on reference spectral libraries, but the chemical space covered by existing databases remains incomplete relative to the vast structural diversity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) expected in the interstellar medium. We present a large-scale, high-throughput PAH infrared (IR) spectral database that complements existing reference libraries by providing significantly more continuous coverage of the PAH chemical space for small to medium-sized PAHs. We used a machine-learning double-harmonic (ML-DH) framework that integrates neural network force fields with electronic dipole models. This framework achieves quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. It has been validated against independent density functional theory calculations and benchmark spectral databases. The resulting dataset comprises 144,111 IR spectra for 48,037 closed-shell, even-carbon benzenoid PAH structures across neutral, cationic, and anionic charge states, complete with per-spectrum uncertainty estimates. The spectral library, optimized geometries, and model code are publicly available. They can be used to complement existing libraries for interpreting and modeling JWST AIB observations and those from future IR missions.

title: An Energetic Consistency Test for Feedback-Driven Gas Loss in Milky Way Dwarf Satellites
abstract: Dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) contain little detectable cold gas, but the relative roles of stellar feedback, reionization, and environmental effects in their gas loss remain uncertain. We apply an order-of-magnitude energy-budget test to nine Milky Way dwarf satellites using published color--magnitude-diagram star formation histories (SFHs), galaxy-level velocity dispersions, effective radii, and integrated $V$-band luminosities. For each galaxy and halo prescription, we define the energy-equivalence time $τ_{\mathrm{E}}$, when a crossing exists, as the first elapsed time at which the cumulative effective energy from core-collapse supernovae equals the adopted gas binding energy. This quantity is an energetic diagnostic rather than a direct measurement of wind launch. Under the fiducial parameters, all nine galaxies reach the nominal threshold under the kinematic--size prescription K+B16, yet star formation often continues long after threshold crossing. We compare the corresponding lookback time $t_{\mathrm{E,lb}}$ with $t_{90,\mathrm{lb}}$, the lookback time at which 90\% of the total initial stellar mass had formed. Because both times are derived from the same cumulative SFH, their temporal proximity is interpreted descriptively rather than as independent evidence of feedback-driven quenching. Whether the threshold is reached depends on the adopted halo mass, radius, retained gas fraction, and supernova--gas coupling efficiency. These results distinguish the availability of sufficient cumulative feedback energy from the processes that determine the timing of quenching.

title: ALMA observations towards M83 reveal N2H+ tracing dense gas
abstract: Galactic observations have shown that N2H+ intensities preferentially trace star-forming dense molecular gas compared with HCN or HCO+, which are conventionally used as dense-gas tracers in extragalactic studies. In this study, we aim to verify this trend in the nearby star-forming galaxy M83. Using ALMA, we observed the J=1-0 transitions of N2H+ and HCN, along with the 1-mm and 3-mm continuum, and analyzed the archival CO(1-0) data. The data achieved a spatial resolution of 48 pc in the southwestern bar-end region of M83, covering an area of 2.1 kpc x 1.8 kpc. N2H+ and HCN intensities are approximately linearly correlated, indicating that HCN luminosity can still reasonably predict the amount of dense gas as well as N2H+ luminosity does. However, in regions with high column densities, N2H+ becomes a super-linear function of HCN, suggesting that the N2H+ emission is more sensitive to dense gas than HCN. We employed a radiative transfer model that predicts line intensities as a function of column density, adopting parametric column density probability distribution functions (N-PDFs) to describe the underlying column density distribution. The model demonstrates that the observed linear or superlinear trend can be explained by a log-normal distribution only or a log-normal and a power-law tail distribution in the N-PDF. Furthermore, the N2H+ intensity is significantly more sensitive to the power-law tail than the HCN intensity. In addition, our analysis incorporating archival data shows that N2H+ is a less reliable tracer of dense gas in galactic center regions, where warmer temperatures may promote N2H+ destruction.

title: Detecting and Identifying Supernovae in AGN Accretion Disks
abstract: Stars may become embedded in active galactic nucleus (AGN) accretion disks and eventually explode as supernovae (SNe), whose detection would provide direct evidence for the existence and evolution of stars in AGN disks. We investigate the electromagnetic emission of such disk SNe using an analytic shock dynamics model coupled with a one-zone radiation model. Applying this framework to four progenitor types over a range of AGN black hole masses and Eddington ratios, we find that disk SNe around lower-mass black holes (BHs) or at lower Eddington ratios are more readily detectable against the underlying AGN emission and can remain detectable over a broader range of electromagnetic bands, from the infrared to soft X-rays. However, detectability against the AGN background does not guarantee that disk SNe can be distinguished from isolated SNe with CSM interaction. We therefore further compare disk SNe with isolated SNe with and without CSM interaction and find substantial degeneracies in their macroscopic observables. Nevertheless, we identify distinctive signatures that are robust across progenitor types. The characteristic emission shifts from the EUV for \(M_{\rm BH}\lesssim10^7\,M_\odot\) toward the UV/optical for \(M_{\rm BH}=10^8\,M_\odot\), with the visibility timescale increasing from less than a day to \(\sim3\text{--}70\) days and \(T_{\rm peak}\sim3\text{--}8\) eV in the latter case. The UV/optical regime around \(10^8\,M_\odot\) BHs therefore offers particularly promising prospects for detecting disk SNe.

title: Testing the inelastic dark matter interpretation of the LZ event with heavy-element experiments
abstract: We consider the inelastic dark matter interpretation of the recent 248 keV event observed by LZ and identify different experiments that could test it. Details of the underlying model and the ability of complementary experiments to test it depend significantly on the high-velocity tail of the dark matter distribution. We consider several example velocity distributions motivated by the impact of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) in order to map out the effects of this dependence. For example, we illustrate the type of high-velocity tail that would make the thermal Higgsino viable despite stringent constraints from solar neutrinos: Reducing the flux of the tail relative to simulation results improves the Higgsino fit, while extending the tail to higher velocities at fluxes below current simulation resolution evades the solar neutrino bound. This motivates more detailed simulations at higher resolution to understand the tail better. Even if xenon experiments confirm the signal event, complementary experiments are still required to test whether the underlying model is inelastic dark matter and to break degeneracies in the measurement of dark matter parameters such as mass and mass splitting. Heavy-element paleodetectors could cover most of the parameter space relevant to the LZ event. Their use of different elements could determine the dark matter mass and splitting, while their unique sensitivity to the history of the dark matter distribution could test the signal's LMC origin. Luminous detection in large neutrino detectors with heavy-element supplements could directly test the inelastic nature of the signal and measure the mass splitting, while its sensitivity to the radiative decay rate could provide strong evidence for the Higgsino interpretation.

title: ACACIAS II: element abundances for 39 stars in the dwarf galaxy Sculptor
abstract: Element abundances in nearby galaxies provide insights into their chemical enrichment histories and place the Milky Way and its neighbours in a broader cosmological context. These systems can be studied through individual stars, whose resolved spectra enable the construction of a chemical abundance census of the Local Group. We present the second stage of the ACACIAS (extra-galactic ArChAeology with Cannon Inferred Abundances from resolved integral field unit Spectra) program, which aims to build the first homogeneous data set of stellar abundances across dwarf galaxies spanning a range of masses for comparison with Milky Way properties. We analyse low-resolution (R=1800), low-SNR (signal-to-noise ratio, ~ 25) MUSE spectra for 39 stars in the Sculptor dwarf spheroidal galaxy. Using the data-driven method The Cannon, we combine high-fidelity labels from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) survey with MUSE-like Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) spectra to analyse the MUSE data. This enables the determination of [Mg/Fe], [Mn/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], and [Al/Fe] on the APOGEE abundance scale, with precisions of σ = 0.09-0.37 dex. Comparing model configurations, we show that [Mg/Fe], [Mn/Fe], and [C/Fe] are best recovered from targeted spectral windows, whereas stellar parameters and [Al/Fe] benefit from full-spectrum information with telluric masking. This reflects the complementary strengths of restricted-window models, which recover abundances from direct spectral features, and full-spectrum models, which exploit correlations with other labels when diagnostic features are weak or absent. Our approach demonstrates the potential of low-resolution, low-SNR stellar spectra to build homogeneous datasets for extragalactic archaeology to better understand the chemical enrichment diversity of the Local Group.

title: JWST reveals a highly ionized nebula powered by an ultraluminous X-ray source with a massive black hole in the metal-poor galaxy Holmberg II
abstract: Recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have revealed fine-structure lines of ions with ionization potentials ${\gtrsim}50$\,eV, such as [Ne\,{\sc v}] and [O\,{\sc iv}], in nebular spectra of some low-metallicity galaxies, raising questions about the nature of the ionizing sources. Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) have been considered as potential contributors, but direct evidence linking individual ULXs to highly ionized nebulae is limited. Here we present JWST IFU spectroscopy of the nebula surrounding the template ULX Ho\,II\,X--1 in the low-metallicity galaxy Holmberg\,II, already known to emit He\,{\sc ii}\,$\lambda4686$ and [O\,{\sc iv}]\,25.89\,$μ$m lines. We resolve the infrared nebula on spatial scales of ${\sim}15-25$\,pc and report the first detections of [Ne\,{\sc v}] and [Ne\,{\sc vi}] in this source. We find anisotropic ionizing conditions: emission from the highest-ionization species arises from compact regions offset from the ULX toward the previously detected radio knots, whereas lower-ionization species trace the wider nebula. The preferential alignment of the highest-ionization emission with the radio axis suggests anisotropic escape of the ionizing continuum and a physical connection with jet-ejection activity. Spectral lines across the nebula are narrow and consistent with the instrumental resolution, indicating kinematically quiescent gas and disfavoring shocks as the dominant ionization mechanism. Together, these results provide direct evidence linking an individual ULX to a highly ionized nebula in a low-metallicity galaxy. These JWST observations of Ho~II~X--1 show that an accreting black hole in a low-metallicity galaxy is responsible for the extreme ionization of the surrounding nebula on ${\sim}100$\,pc scales.

title: Self Calibrated Galaxy Groups from the DESI DR1 Bright Galaxy Survey
abstract: We present a galaxy group catalog built from Data Release 1 of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey, using the Self Calibrated Group Finder. The algorithm uses clustering data from the observed sample to calibrate the Group Finder's free parameters, rather than simulations. The catalog contains 2,229,741 galaxies from ~$2680$ deg$^2$ of sky with 3-pass coverage and $r$-band fluxes $\lt 19.5$. The catalog classifies all galaxies in the flux-limited sample as centrals or satellites and estimates host dark matter halo masses. We show the satellite fraction $f_{\rm sat}$, luminosity halo mass relation, stellar halo mass relation and halo occupation distributions (HODs) from the catalog. We find these non-parametric HODs can be fit by standard HOD models, with satellite power-law index $α$ values around 0.75 for star-forming galaxies and around 1.1 for quiescent objects. In agreement with recent results, we find that the quenched fraction of central galaxies depends mostly on halo mass and is nearly independent of central galaxy stellar mass for galaxies more massive than $10^{10.3}$ $M_\odot h^{-1}$ and halos more massive than $10^{12.2}$ $M_\odot h^{-1}$. In an appendix, we introduce a new Hybrid Nearest Neighbor (HNN) technique to mitigate systematics from fiber incompleteness. HNN uses photometric redshifts and multiple on-sky neighbors to assign redshifts to unobserved targets. Calibrated on DESI Survey Validation 3 data, our technique yields correct redshifts $\sim 50\%$ of the time and produces unbiased halo occupation statistics.

title: Unveiling the Baryon Cycle Through Cosmic Time
abstract: Galaxy evolution is governed by the baryon cycle: gas accreted from the cosmic web and circumgalactic medium condenses into molecular gas, forms stars, and is redistributed by stellar and AGN feedback. Tracing the molecular phase is therefore essential to understanding how galaxies acquire, consume, and eject their baryons. Yet current molecular-gas surveys remain limited by sensitivity, area, cosmic variance, and spectral bandwidth. ALMA2040 would combine a $\sim10\times$ sensitivity improvement with $\gtrsim512$ GHz simultaneous frequency coverage, delivering $\sim100\times$ faster mapping at fixed depth and a further $\gtrsim25\times$ gain in instantaneous bandwidth. Together, these advances would increase spectroscopic survey speed by orders of magnitude, enabling tiered ``wedding-cake'' strategies: an ultra-deep $\sim4$-5 arcmin$^2$ field probing faint and high-redshift reservoirs, a $\sim$0.25 deg$^2$ survey reaching molecular-line sensitivities comparable to current ultra-deep fields over a much larger cosmological volume, and thousands of independent pointings minimizing cosmic variance. Broad spectral coverage would simultaneously detect multiple CO transitions, [CI], H$_2$O, feedback tracers, far-IR fine-structure lines, and dust continuum, constraining molecular gas, ISM conditions, obscured star formation, and gas flows within the same observations. Every targeted observation would also become a molecular deep field, extending these measurements to serendipitous galaxies. Together with future HI, optical, and near-IR surveys, ALMA2040 would enable a population-resolved view of the baryon cycle across cosmic time and stringent tests of galaxy formation models.

title: The optical colors of hidden spiral-like features in nine Virgo early--type dwarfs
abstract: Dwarf early-type galaxies (ETGs) are abundant in nearby clusters and provide a key laboratory for studying environmentally driven galaxy transformation. Although dwarf ETGs were once considered structurally simple, deep imaging has revealed embedded spiral-like features (e.g., bars and spiral arms) in some of them, contributing only a small fraction of the total light. Their origin at dwarf scales remains uncertain. As a pilot study, we investigate spiral-like features in nine Virgo dwarf ETGs with clear embedded arms, using optical colors to test whether these features differ from the surrounding diffuse component, which would constrain their formation pathways. Using deep g- and i-band NGVS images, we apply a residual-based method to separate excess light associated with the spiral-like component from the diffuse host. The residual images define arm and interarm regions, enabling direct measurements of light fractions and g-i colors for both components. The spiral-like features contribute only a few percent of the total light (about 1.5-5.5% in i and 1.7-3.7% in g). We find a diverse range of colors across the sample: four galaxies host spiral-like features redder than their interarm regions, four show no robust arm-interarm color difference, and one exhibits a distinctly bluer spiral-like component. The latter is consistent with a recently quenched transition object, while the redder and color-uniform features are consistent with older or more metal-rich stellar populations. Spiral-like features in Virgo dwarf ETGs thus exhibit a surprising diversity in their photometric properties, implying multiple evolutionary channels rather than a single one. This pilot analysis also demonstrates readiness for the much larger NGVS sample of dwarfs with potential spiral-like features.

title: What fuels the growth of stars and black holes in galaxies through cosmic time? The physics and chemistry of the interstellar medium in distant galaxies
abstract: The interplay between the baryonic matter in galaxies (gas, dust, stars) has a fundamental role in our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution through cosmic time. The (sub)mm regime provides a unique window to measure the physical conditions and chemistry in the cold and dusty gas reservoirs that fuel the formation of new stars and the growth of massive black holes in distant galaxies. Large sub(mm) interferometers have made a revolutionary impact mapping the cold gas and dust in galaxies beyond the local universe. However, significant progress is hampered by limited spectral-line sensitivity. After more than a decade of surveys, molecular gas (traced by 12CO) has been measured only in a few tens of typical, massive main-sequence star-forming galaxies at z>1, while access to fainter gas-tracing species has been limited to only the very brightest galaxies. Thereby it restricts access to the detailed conditions in the cold gas clouds in typical galaxies in the distant universe. A revolutionary, flagship sub-mm interferometer with a massive increase in instantaneous spectral line sensitivity and broad spectral grasp (ALMA2040) fills this gap by enabling rich, multi-transition, multi-species and multi-isotopologue studies of the atomic and molecular interstellar medium for thousands of typical galaxies across galaxy populations and redshift. This will unveil how the ISM evolves across the galaxy population for statistical samples in different redshift bins, detailed studies of the physical conditions and chemistry in the multi-phase interstellar medium of typical galaxies, and how the cold ISM regulates and responds to star- and black-hole formation, providing a tremendous leap forward in the study of galaxy assembly over cosmic time.

title: The ALMA-QUARKS Survey. IV. Core Mass Function and Evolutionary Trends in Core Formation Efficiency and Chemistry
abstract: The ALMA-QUARKS (Querying Underlying Mechanisms of Massive Star Formation with ALMA-Resolved Gas Kinematics and Structures) survey targets 139 massive protoclusters selected from the ATOMS survey. The targets were observed at 1.3~mm wavelength with an angular resolution of $\sim0.3^{\prime\prime}$, corresponding to $\sim10^3$~au at the sample's median distance of $\sim3.8$~kpc. Using \texttt{getsf}, we identify 3374 dense cores and classify them as starless, protostellar, hot core, or H{\sc ii} region candidates based on spectral-line diagnostics (e.g., H30$α$, CH$_3$CN, and CH$_3$OH) and CO outflow associations. The resulting catalog provides core physical properties and enables statistical investigations of dense core populations in massive protocluster environments. The derived global core mass function (CMF) after excluding H{\sc ii} region candidates, which is biased by distance effects, has a relatively flat power-law slope at the high-mass end ($\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}\log M \propto M^{-γ}$, with $γ=0.98\pm0.03$). In contrast, the measured high-mass slopes in individual distance bins are approximately Salpeter-like, while their fitted lower mass limits increase with distance. We further examine the core formation efficiency (CFE) across the full sample and find that it positively correlates with the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the parental clumps, consistent with an evolutionary increase in the fraction of mass concentrated into dense cores. We also investigate the detection rates of different molecular tracers and find systematic chemical variations with evolutionary stage. Compared with the ASHES survey, we find that the detection rates of deuterated species vary significantly even for cores at the same evolutionary stages, suggesting an important environmental influence on the chemical evolution of cores.

title: A Search for Dust in the Outflow of the HH212 Class 0 Protostellar System
abstract: Perhaps the most visually striking phenomenon during star formation is the ejection of material along the direction of the protostar's rotational axis. Observed in the form of molecular outflows and/or atomic jets, these features carry away mass, energy and angular momentum from the system. Given the known dust content of protoplanetary disks, and the energetics of outflows, it has been suggested that it should be possible to lift dust from disks via winds, yet limited observational evidence has been presented in the literature. Any detection of dust within protostellar outflows not only puts constraints on the dust content in outflows, but if a sufficient amount of dust can be removed from the system, the mass budget for planet formation could also be affected. We present re-imaging of archival, multi-frequency dust continuum observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) towards the HH212 protostellar system. We detect an extension in the dust emission, and using multi-frequency data in Bands 7 and 9, we estimate the spectral index of the emitting dust and the dust mass in the wind launching region. We find a small but still significant amount of dust mass coincident with the molecular outflow cavity. This finding is assessed in relation to the hypothesis that the outflow could be capable of transporting dust away from the HH212 protoplanetary disk.

title: The dawn of the first galaxies
abstract: Understanding how the first galaxies assembled their stellar mass at cosmic dawn is a central frontier of modern astrophysics. JWST has now revealed an unexpected population of ultraviolet-bright galaxies at z>10, whose intense emission points towards a rapid stellar mass growth that challenges current models of early galaxy assembly. Yet, the cold gas fueling this growth remains hidden: current ALMA sensitivity restricts routine detection to only the brightest ionized-gas tracers such as [OIII] 88$μ$m, while [CII] 158$μ$m, a key coolant and gas-mass proxy of the neutral interstellar medium (ISM), is undetected beyond $z\sim8$. This leaves fundamental questions unanswered: how quickly primeval galaxies gathered cold gas and turned it into stars; what physical conditions (density, temperature, radiation field) characterized their ISM; how fast metals and dust built up; and how feedback regulated early gas assembly. Only a transformational sub-millimeter facility like ALMA2040 can address these questions, enabling systematic surveys of [CII] in the first galaxies and providing a representative census of gas fractions and depletion times. A simulated galaxy at $z=11.3$ shows that ALMA2040 not only will detect, but also spatially resolve its merging cold-gas structure in [CII] on $\sim$200 pc scales in 5 hours (below 100 pc in 10 hours). ALMA2040 will also spectrally resolve multiple lines simultaneously, akin to integral-field spectroscopy, providing the key diagnostics needed to break density-metallicity-radiation-field degeneracies and map the multi-phase ISM of z>10 galaxies. The combination of dramatically increased line sensitivity and wide instantaneous bandwidth will push the search for the first galaxies out to the earliest cosmic times, with [OIII] detectable up to $z\sim20$. ALMA2040 will thus be transformative for understanding how the first galaxies assembled at cosmic dawn.

title: A model for the ongoing subcluster interaction in Centaurus
abstract: Intracluster globular clusters (GCs) preserve the hierarchical and chemical history of galaxy cluster assembly. The nearby Centaurus cluster is believed to be undergoing an interaction between two subclusters, Cen 30 and Cen 45, which should leave an imprint on its intracluster GCs. We aim to characterise the GC population in Centaurus and constrain its recent assembly history, ultimately constructing an interaction scenario consistent with the observational evidence. Using deep VLT/FORS imaging in the $V$ and $I$ bands, we select GC candidates around the cluster centre based on morphology and colour criteria. We use a Voronoi tessellation approach to study the GC spatial distribution and density profiles, demonstrating its advantages over traditional annuli-based methods. We then constrain the evolution of the galaxy luminosity function using the GC specific frequency and colour distribution. The GC spatial distribution shows significant substructure. As in other clusters, red GCs are concentrated on the brightest galaxies, whereas blue GCs trace a more extended structure. We confirm and quantify the previously reported 'bridge' of GCs connecting NGC 4696 and NGC 4709, showing that it hosts twice as many GCs as expected from the projected GC systems of the two galaxies alone. The inferred evolution of the galaxy luminosity function agrees with previous results for Hydra I, yielding a faint-end slope of $α=-1.87_{-0.06}^{+0.06}$ for the galaxy population that assembled the Centaurus core. We propose a nearly head-on collision scenario in which Cen 45 recently passed through Cen 30, with the two subclusters moving approximately along the line of sight. This scenario explains the large line-of-sight velocity difference between the subclusters, the hot X-ray-emitting gas between them, the GC bridge, and the puffed-up GC system of NGC 4709.

title: Has JWST Seen Everything? Hunting for "NIRCam-dark" Dusty Star-Forming Galaxies at $z \simeq 6 - 9$ with ALMA2040
abstract: JWST/NIRCam has recovered the stellar counterparts of many ALMA-detected, formerly HST-dark galaxies, yet ALMA has started identifying dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) at $z>6$ that remain extremely faint or undetected even with NIRCam. These "NIRCam-dark" DSFGs may trace a missing rapid-growth phase connecting UV-luminous galaxies at $z>10$ to massive quiescent galaxies at $z\gtrsim4$. So far, the small, heterogeneously selected NIRCam-dark sample is insufficient to determine their abundance or role in the evolution of massive galaxies. We show that a blind 1.3-mm continuum survey with ALMA2040 can provide the first high-significance census of this elusive NIRCam-dark DSFG population across $z\simeq 6 - 9$. We conduct sensitivity and survey-speed calculations requiring a $10σ$ detection of a NIRCam-dark DSFG with a dust-obscured star-formation rate of $60\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ at $z = 8$. At a like-for-like 7.5-GHz normalization, ALMA2040 will reach the required 1.3-mm RMS of $21\,μ$Jy beam$^{-1}$ about 90 times faster than current ALMA. With 100 hr on-source, ALMA2040 can cover an area of $\sim0.5$ deg$^2$ and detect $\langle N \rangle\sim16$ NIRCam-dark DSFGs over $7.5<z<9$, assuming a fiducial number density $n=3\times10^{-6}$ cMpc$^{-3}$. Dividing the survey among independent fields with deep JWST coverage would mitigate cosmic variance and enable immediate NIRCam, MIRI, and spectroscopic characterization of their environments. The $\geq512$-GHz instantaneous bandwidth expected for ALMA2040 will also detect [C II] line at a wide redshift range, supplementing the continuum discovery with redshift confirmation. Such a survey will test whether NIRCam-dark DSFGs trace a missing rapid-growth phase between the earliest UV-luminous galaxies at $z>10$ and the rapid emergence of massive quiescent systems at $z\gtrsim 4$.

title: ALMA2040: Understanding the Early Assembly of Galaxies - The Formation of Star-Forming Clumps and their Role in Shaping Galaxy Evolution
abstract: Astrophysics seeks to explain how galaxies form and evolve through the interplay of stars, gas, and dust. Giant molecular clouds (GMCs), the main reservoirs and sites of star formation, link the cold interstellar medium to the birth of stars and stellar structures. Their properties reflect galactic disk conditions, and their evolution is shaped by stellar feedback and host-galaxy dynamics. Studying GMCs across cosmic time is therefore key to understanding how gas turns into stars and drives galaxy evolution. Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope observations reveal compact star-forming clumps in galaxies from Cosmic Noon to the Epoch of Reionization ($z\approx6$), but their link to the molecular gas reservoir is still unclear. We do not yet know how GMC properties vary with redshift and environment, how molecular gas, dust, and young stars are arranged, or whether clumps form in unstable disks or disturbed systems. Addressing these questions requires spatially resolved observations of the cold interstellar medium at the scales probed by optical/near-infrared facilities. ALMA2040, a transformational next-generation sub-mm facility, will provide the sensitivity and angular resolution needed to detect individual GMCs in representative lensed and unlensed galaxies at $z>1$. CO and [CII], complemented by dust continuum and molecular-gas kinematics, will measure the molecular gas reservoir, its physical conditions, and its dynamical state. Together with JWST and the ELT, ALMA2040 will connect cold gas, dust, and stellar structures across cosmic time. ALMA2040 will revolutionize our understanding of (i) the properties and evolution of GMCs and their connection to star-forming clumps, (ii) the spatial interplay between molecular gas, dust, and young stars, and (iii) the dynamics, survival, and formation of GMCs and stellar clumps.

title: An Attenuation Bump at z=9.3: Probing Dust Diversity at Cosmic Dawn
abstract: We report the identification of a UV attenuation bump in the Black Pearl, a galaxy at a spectroscopic redshift of 9.3335 observed with JWST/NIRSpec as part of the ZENITH and EMBER surveys. This is the highest-redshift UV bump reported to date, probing dust properties only approximately 500 Myr after the Big Bang. The feature is directly detected as a broad depression in the rest-frame UV continuum and is well described by a local Drude profile, with a central wavelength of 2132+/-17 Angstroms, an FWHM of 413+/-54 Angstroms, and a peak attenuation of 0.21+/-0.02 mag. Joint spectrophotometric modeling with a flexible attenuation law independently recovers a pronounced UV bump without imposing its presence a priori, regardless of the adopted star-formation history. The modeling indicates a relatively low-mass, actively star-forming galaxy, with a logarithmic stellar mass of 8.35 (+0.09/-0.08) in solar units, a star-formation rate of 2.36 (+0.54/-0.42) solar masses per year, and a visual attenuation of 0.34 (+0.12/-0.11) mag. Rest-frame optical emission-line diagnostics indicate a hard ionizing spectrum and allow for a moderate AGN contribution, but provide no evidence for a powerful AGN capable of dominating the observed UV continuum. The bump is blueshifted by 43+/-17 Angstroms (approximately 2.5 sigma) relative to the canonical Milky Way 2175 Angstrom feature and by 127 +/- 17 Angstroms relative to the few UV bumps currently known at redshift approximately 7, while its width is consistent with the broad distribution measured along Milky Way sightlines. The displaced central wavelength therefore provides the clearest evidence for a nonstandard UV-bump profile at redshift 9.3335, pointing to substantial diversity in the properties of UV-bump carriers at early cosmic times, with both PAHs and small graphite grains remaining plausible candidates.

title: Wandering intermediate-mass black holes and off-nuclear tidal disruption events from early star clusters
abstract: Off-nuclear tidal disruption events (TDEs) reveal evidence for massive black holes outside galactic centers, but the origins of this wandering population remain uncertain. We investigate wandering intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) formed through runaway stellar collisions in dense, high-redshift star clusters and predict their TDE signatures across cosmic time. Our semi-analytic model samples clusters associated with low-mass subhalos at $7<z<20$ and uses merger trees from the IllustrisTNG TNG50 simulation to follow the assembly of 15 elliptical galaxies with stellar masses of $10^9-10^{11}~M_\odot$. We compare two models for high-redshift cluster formation: a maximal model taken from a high-resolution simulation and a conservative model calibrated from local cluster relations. Off-nuclear TDEs produced through this mechanism occur in bursts within 10-100 Myr of IMBH formation as the loss-cone surrounding the black hole is depleted. We estimate the rate of off-nuclear TDEs expected across time per galaxy, and characterize these events as typically occurring between $10-10^3$ kpc from their host galaxy centers. Event rates increase with galaxy mass; in the maximal model, the progenitors of the most massive galaxies reach peak off-nuclear TDE rates of approximately $5\times10^{-4}-4\times10^{-2}~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ per galaxy at $7\lesssim z\lesssim13$. This work provides a framework for constraining the early population of star clusters that form IMBHs through runaway collapse via their contribution to the rate of off-nuclear TDEs in the high redshift Universe.

title: The Pristine survey XXIX. Data Release 2: Photometric metallicities for 15 millions stars down to $G\sim 20.5$
abstract: Tailored narrow-band photometric observations are an efficient way to measure the metallicity of Milky Way stars. The Pristine survey has been mapping the northern sky since 2015 using narrow-band $CaHK$ photometry obtained with the MegaCam imager on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT). Data Release 1 (DR1) provided a high-precision absolute calibration of the survey observed before October 2022 using \Gaia DR3 XP synthetic photometry, yielding photometric metallicities over $\sim$6,500 deg$^2$, but was limited in depth to the availability of \Gaia spectro-photometry ($G \lesssim 17.65$). We present the Pristine Data Release 2 (DR2) that includes all Pristine observations until January 2025, corresponding to an additional 1,500\,deg$^2$ of coverage, and including all faint sources down to $G\sim20.5$. This release aims to exploit the full depth of the Pristine observations to uncover the faint metal-poor halo. We process all images observed from the start of the survey in March 2015 through to January 2025 following the methodology presented in DR1. The core of the calibration utilizes the subset of bright stars with \Gaia synthetic $CaHK_\mathrm{syn}$ magnitudes to train the \texttt{PhotCalib} neural network. We then derive photometric metallicities using the established Pristine ($CaHK, G, G_{\rm BP}, G_{\rm RP}$) to [Fe/H] model. The resulting catalogue covers approximately $\sim$ 8,000 deg$^{2}$ and provides photometric metallicities for 15 millions FGK stars, which show good agreement with recently published, independent Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) metallicities. With its increased coverage and access to a significantly fainter regime compared to DR1, DR2 significantly increases the volume of the survey. We report more than 200,000 and 6,500 very and extremely metal-poor star candidates, respectively.

title: HI rotation curves and mass-size relation for 568 galaxies from the Apertif Wide-area Extragalactic Survey
abstract: The extended HI rotation curves of galaxies are one of the most powerful tools for studying galaxy evolution and for testing different dark matter and modified gravity models. However, their sample sizes have historically been limited to a few hundred galaxies, mostly due to the survey speed of radio interferometers. Here, we present a first data release of HI kinematic models from the Apertif Wide-area Extragalactic Survey (AWES). Starting from 1924 galaxies detected in HI, we constructed 568 reliable kinematic models, which provide rotation curves, velocity dispersion profiles, surface density profiles, and HI disk geometries. This dataset constitutes the largest homogeneous HI rotation curve sample to date. The HI disks of the modeled galaxies span three orders of magnitude in HI mass, have outer rotation velocities between ~20 and ~300 km/s, and extend from 2 to more than 60 kpc. The number of data points of the rotation curves ranges from 3 to 23, with a peak value at 4 and a broad tail to larger values. The rotation curves display a variety of inner shapes, but in general, they tend to become flat at large radii. Based on the HI surface density profiles derived during the kinematic modeling, we studied the HI mass-size relation with a large homogeneous sample of 213 galaxies. The relation is very tight, with an observed scatter along the mass direction of ~0.101 dex and an inferred intrinsic scatter along the same direction of only 0.067 +/- 0.007 dex. The best fitting slope is 1.96 +/- 0.03 when fitting for mass as a function of size, indicating that HI disks have a constant average surface density.

title: Probing ordered magnetic fields in galaxies across cosmic time
abstract: Magnetic fields are dynamically important across many astronomical environments, yet their origin, strength, and evolution over cosmic time remain poorly understood. Ordered magnetic fields are ubiquitous in the nearby Universe, as revealed by a range of observational techniques, but evidence for their existence at cosmological distances is scarce. Recent ALMA detections of polarised dust emission indicate that galactic-scale ordered magnetic fields, spanning up to kiloparsec scales, were already present in massive star-forming galaxies at redshifts up to $z\sim5.6$. This white paper argues that the ALMA2040 concept -- with its nearly tenfold improvement in sensitivity and angular resolution, and full-polarisation capability extended to higher-frequency bands -- will open up the study of cosmic magnetism in the early Universe. We identify four science drivers: constraining the dynamos that generate galactic-scale ordered fields, measuring the strength of early magnetic fields, connecting magnetic fields to galaxy evolution across cosmic time, and constraining dust grain properties through the polarised spectral energy distribution. We summarise the corresponding requirements in angular resolution, spectral coverage, and sensitivity, and discuss synergies with next-generation telescopes.

title: How Little Red Dots Turn Blue: Evolution of Kelvin-Helmholtz Contracting Black Hole Envelopes and Observational Diagnostics
abstract: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have revealed compact, red-colored, broad-line emitters known as little red dots (LRDs), while a bluer counterpart population has been referred to as little blue dots (LBDs). Their physical connection remains unclear: they may represent different evolutionary stages of the same phenomenon, distinct populations, or different phases of the broader evolution of early galaxies and their black holes (BHs). We propose a model in which a rapidly growing BH is embedded in a geometrically thick gaseous envelope accompanied by concurrent nuclear star formation. The model reproduces the observed spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of LRDs and LBDs, and naturally connects the two phases through Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction of the envelope and exposure of the nuclear accretion disk, as the gas supply declines due to external stellar activity or feedback. We predict the corresponding evolutionary tracks in the UV-optical slope ($β_{\rm UV}$-$β_{\rm opt}$) plane which bridge the apparent gap between LRDs and LBDs. These evolutionary tracks start from the LRD regime and consistently exhibit a red excursion that extends toward $(β_{\rm UV},β_{\rm opt})\sim(2,-1)$ before turning toward the LBD regime. This feature is largely insensitive to variations in the model parameters that govern the envelope structure, providing a robust signature of the transitional population. The transition lasts $\sim5$-$50\,\mathrm{Myr}$, depending primarily on the BH feedback efficiency and the gas-retention efficiency of the envelope. The abundance ratio of transitional systems to LRDs therefore provides a constraint on BH feedback and gas retention during the rapid growth of early supermassive BHs.

title: Tracing small-scale structure formation through cosmic time with strong gravitational lensing: A case for a next-generation sub-millimetre/millimetre interferometer
abstract: The nature of dark matter and the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remain major open questions in modern astrophysics. Both leave a key signature in an overlapping, largely unexplored mass range: $<10^7$ M$_{\odot}$ dark haloes and wandering black holes. These may be undetectable directly, but detectable through gravitational perturbation of strongly lensed images, and partly or entirely distinguishable from one another through lensing data alone. We demonstrate through realistic simulations that a 255-element sub-mm/mm interferometer could probe this critical mass regime, detecting gravitational perturbations in strongly lensed dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) from objects down to at least $10^5$ M$_{\odot}$. Combined with lens-galaxy characterisation from the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), which strengthens the physical interpretation of detected perturbers, and the unprecedented lens samples expected from Euclid and the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), this facility could deliver a census of low-mass dark matter haloes and wandering massive black holes across cosmic time.

title: The Impact of High-Mass Clusters on the Binary Black Hole Merger Rate over Cosmic Time
abstract: We present a cosmological calculation of the binary black hole merger rate from dense star clusters, using a $\texttt{Cluster Monte Carlo}$ ($\texttt{CMC}$) model grid spanning the full observed parameter space of cluster mass, metallicity, and virial radius. For the first time, we incorporate $N=10^{7}$-particle $\texttt{CMC}$ models into this calculation, including a new solar-metallicity model, extending the $\texttt{CMC Cluster Catalog}$ to the most massive clusters observed in the local Universe. Using an analytic cluster formation model which convolves the cluster formation rate with delay-time distributions from our model suite, we find that the local cluster BBH merger rate is dominated by low-mass ($M_1 \lesssim 20\,M_\odot$) mergers originating from recently formed, high-metallicity clusters. While high-mass clusters are the primary sites of hierarchical (second-generation and higher) mergers, their contribution to the overall merger rate is suppressed by the exponential cutoff of the cluster initial mass function. The hierarchical merger rate is therefore highly sensitive to the exact value of the Schechter mass, $M_S$, suggesting that gravitational wave constraints on the hierarchical merger fraction can independently constrain the high-mass end of the cluster initial mass function. Our cluster formation model reproduces the observed present-day GC number density without fine tuning, and we find $M_S = 10^7\,M_\odot$ provides the best match to the observed Virgo GC mass distribution. For this value, $27\%$ of local dynamical mergers are hierarchical, compared to $18\%$ for the canonical value of $M_S = 10^{6.26}\,M_\odot$. Our merger weights, which we make publicly available, can be used for direct comparison with LVK distributions and other formation models.

title: Efficient numerical evolution of self-gravitating systems with dark-matter-baryon scattering
abstract: We present a fast algorithm to numerically evolve a spherically symmetric system consisting of dark matter and gas, including dark-matter-baryon scattering. The method augments the spherical N-body code NSphere, which collapses the six-dimensional phase space of a spherical collisionless system to three dimensions, with a one-dimensional Lagrangian treatment of gas. Dark-matter-baryon scattering is implemented as a Monte-Carlo process between the dark-matter numerical particles and the gas shells. We also implement an algorithm for radiative gas cooling that is valid for weak cooling. The gas, as well as dark-matter-baryon scattering and cooling, adds only incrementally to the run time of the code, allowing systems to be evolved on a laptop computer, a tiny fraction of the computational resources required for a full 3D N-body/hydro simulation. To illustrate, we show the evolution of a $\sim 10^{13}\,M_\odot$ halo with a dark-matter-baryon scattering cross section $σ_{\rm tot}/m_χ=0.1\,{\rm cm}^2\,{\rm g}^{-1}$ but no gas cooling. We then show examples with radiative gas cooling where the cooling is altered through interaction with dark-matter particles. The resulting code, NSphere-IDM, allows the implications of dark-matter interactions for galaxy evolution to be explored quickly over large volumes of the dark-matter parameter space, and other new physics (e.g., dark-matter self-interactions or anisotropy in the distribution function) is easily incorporated. The code can also provide useful calibrations and benchmarks for fully 3D N-body or hydrodynamical simulations.

title: The impact of nonlinear Landau damping on cosmic ray streaming and the role of external turbulence
abstract: Cosmic rays (CRs) streaming faster than the Alfvén speed generate Alfvén waves that scatter them. The saturated wave amplitude is regulated by a damping mechanism. This damping controls the CR scattering rate and drift velocity, and thus the rate at which CRs transfer momentum and energy to the ambient plasma, which sets the strength of CR feedback. In the ionized interstellar medium, nonlinear Landau damping (NLLD) is commonly invoked as the dominant damping mechanism for Alfvén waves. We test this assumption with fluid-PIC simulations in which thermal ions and electrons are modeled as fluids with optional Landau closures, allowing us to compare otherwise identical runs with and without NLLD. When waves are self-generated by monoenergetic CRs, runs with and without Landau closures are indistinguishable: NLLD is inefficient and the CRs isotropize in the wave frame. Once high-amplitude Alfvén waves mimicking external turbulence are seeded, NLLD curbs wave growth and equalizes forward- and backward-propagating waves. We show that the saturated drift velocity, which falls below the Alfvén speed, can be accurately predicted from the wave spectra alone. If the CR distribution is undersampled, a numerical instability corrupts the largest resonant scales: unphysical, unresolved pitch-angle gradients resonantly generate backward-propagating waves, driving an inverse cascade that should be absent from purely streaming-driven waves. While power-law CR distributions may permit stronger NLLD, our results indicate that NLLD is unlikely to be an intrinsic saturation mechanism of the streaming instability; instead, its effectiveness hinges on the interplay of streaming-generated modes with those of external origin.

title: CoRGI in MaNGA - II. NGC 5717: cold-gas accretion and disk growth in a BGG
abstract: Large-scale stellar counter-rotation, in which two coplanar stellar components rotate in opposite directions, is usually interpreted as a signature of external gas accretion. Such systems are most often found in relatively sparse environments, where cold gas can be acquired and remain dynamically undisturbed long enough to settle into a disk. It is less clear whether this channel can operate in massive central galaxies, whose group or cluster environments can heat, strip, or perturb cold gas. Here we present NGC 5717, one of the most massive galaxies known to host a counter-rotating stellar disk and the first identified case in a brightest group galaxy. Using integral-field spectroscopy from SDSS-IV Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA), together with CFHT imaging, ancillary HI data, and SDSS/DESI spectroscopy of the surrounding group, we show that the galaxy contains a dynamically cold counter-rotating disk embedded in an old dynamically hot elliptical component. The disk is young ($\sim 1.3$ Gyr), metal-poor ([Fe/H] $\sim -0.7$ dex), extended ($h \sim 2.4$ kpc), and massive ($\log M_\star/M_\odot \sim 9.9$); the associated ionized gas co-rotates with it, while the available HI data indicate no significant remaining reservoir of neutral atomic gas ($\log M_{\mathrm{HI}}/M_\odot \lesssim 9$). These properties support an in situ origin of the secondary component from externally accreted gas. The chemical evolution model favors gas accretion from a cosmic filament, which is consistent with the surrounding cosmic-web geometry, and indicates highly efficient burst-like star formation with substantial metal-enriched outflows. NGC 5717 may therefore represent a rare example of disk growth in a massive central galaxy, enabled by external cold-gas accretion during an earlier phase of the group assembly history.

title: A Vision for Little Red Dots in the Low-Redshift Universe with ALMA2040
abstract: The discovery of Little Red Dots (LRDs) at high redshifts with JWST has revealed a previously unknown phase of black-hole growth. However, their black-hole (BH) masses, BH-to-stellar mass ratios, cold-gas reservoirs, and depletion times remain uncertain. The recent discovery of low-redshift LRDs at $z\simeq0.1 - 0.9$ creates a decisive opportunity to access their low-$J$ CO lines for measuring molecular gas reservoirs, and the nearest systems can in principle be spatially resolved. We use J1025+1402 ("The Egg") at $z=0.1007$, the best-studied local LRD, as a benchmark to explore the scientific opportunities with ALMA2040. Assuming a molecular gas mass of $10^9\,M_\odot$, the CO(2-1) detectability strongly depends on the assumed CO-to-H$_2$ conversion ($α_{\rm CO}$). With a large $α_{\rm CO} \simeq 315 - 725\,M_\odot\,({\rm K\,km\,s}^{-1}\,{\rm pc}^2)^{-1}$ at a low gas-phase metallicity, the CO line would remain very challenging for the current ALMA to detect, while ALMA2040 will likely deliver a robust CO detection and thus a gas-reservoir constraint for The Egg. Furthermore, with the best angular resolution at its CO(2-1) frequency (14.6 mas, or 27 pc), ALMA2040 may spatially resolve the CO emission from The Egg. Assuming an optimistic, SMC-like $α_{\rm CO}$ with a 50-hour deep integration, we produce mock position-velocity diagrams that may distinguish a $10^7\,M_\odot$ black hole from the no-BH model through its steeper central velocity structure. We conclude that ALMA2040 has the potential to directly measure the gas masses, depletion times, and excitation of local LRDs, while the CO-bright subset may ultimately yield dynamical constraints on the mass of their central black holes.

title: JWST Observations of RR Lyrae in Leo P
abstract: We analyze co-spatial HST/ACS and JWST/NIRCam time-series photometric observations of RR Lyrae in the low-metallicity dwarf galaxy Leo P. This study provides a new opportunity to explore the properties of and potential for metal-poor RR Lyrae studies with JWST using well-understood relationships from past HST work. We identify 20 RR Lyrae in the HST imaging and 15 RR Lyrae in the JWST imaging. We determine the periods, amplitudes, and mean magnitudes for each of the RR Lyrae. We fit the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity (PWZ) function to the HST RR Lyrae population, and obtain a Gaia-consistent RR Lyrae-based distance to Leo P of $μ= 26.04\pm0.07$ ($1.61\pm0.06$ Mpc), consistent with existing distance measurements. We determine a JWST-based PWZ using Leo P data along with previous JWST RR Lyrae observations in WLM. The simultaneous fit decreases the mean fractional uncertainty by 31% on the slope and by 11% on the intercept, increasing the constraining power as compared to the existing calibration.

title: Binary-lens amplification of starlight: from magnification flares to quasi-periodic tracking of orbital evolution
abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHB) are expected at the center of galaxies as a result of galaxy mergers. The dynamics and evolution of SMBHBs shed light on the evolution and formation of galaxies, the gravitational wave background and the nature of gravity. Many methods have been proposed to identify sub-parsec SMBHBs via the detection of gravitational waves or the modulation of the emission from the surrounding gaseous environment. In a previous study, we proposed a new method of identifying SMBHBs in non-active galactic nuclei via gravitational lensing. The caustics, i.e. the source positions with a divergent magnification, exhibit a complex extended geometry which rotates with the binary period. Each caustic-crossing produces an extreme magnification by up to a factor of $10^{6}$. In this work, we generalize the previous study and describe the rich phenomenology of binary-lens amplification of starlight (BLAST). We explore the electromagnetic transients produced when accounting for the relative proper motion of the source, either a single or a binary star, the eccentricity and precession of the SMBHB, and the relative inclination. Systems where a star rapidly drifts across the caustic produce a single- or double-peaked flare. In the opposite limit, a star with no relative proper motion produces quasi-periodic lensed starlight (QPLS), i.e., repeated peaks that track the system's orbital evolution. We determine the expected magnification and peak duration in different circumstances, and calculate the magnification curves and their Fourier transforms. This study may help construct search pipelines to identify SMBHBs in electromagnetic time-domain surveys.

title: A Parsec-scale Circumstellar Shell Around VX Sgr: Mass Loss and RSG/TŻO Nature
abstract: A thin, arc-shaped shell is discovered surrounding VX Sagittarii (VX Sgr), the largest known CSM shell around an RSG at a scale $r\sim0.59\,\mathrm{pc}$. The nebula has an extinction-corrected H$α$ intensity $I_{\mathrm{H}α}\sim38\,\mathrm{R}$ and an ionized mass $\sim0.1\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$. The slow $12\,\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}$ peculiar velocity of VX Sgr and the lack of far-infrared emission in the arc indicate that it is not produced by a bow shock, but is likely instead steady RSG wind or ejecta that is photoionized by a nearby $\mathrm{O}$- or $\mathrm{B}$- type star. The nature of VX Sgr is debated in the literature as a red supergiant/hypergiant (RSG/RHG), super-AGB star, or Thorne--Żytkow Object (TŻO). Using the kinematic age of the Sgr OB1 association, the super-AGB model is disfavored. A spectroscopic test of the arc is proposed to potentially distinguish an RSG from a possible TŻO. The mass-loss rate is estimated from the geometry and emission measure of the shell, finding $\dot{M}\approx4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The future interaction of the supernova (SN) ejecta of VX Sgr and the surrounding circumstellar material (CSM) is briefly explored through the mass ratio $Λ$ of the shell and SN ejecta; the interaction would likely not have a significant effect on the SN forward shock.

title: Can bosenovae deplete the galactic dark matter?
abstract: No: neither through the bosenovae of gravitational atoms formed around stars and compact objects, nor through those of boson stars formed in the galactic dark-matter halo. We assume that all the dark matter consists of ultralight bosons with attractive self-interactions, which can be captured in the gravitational potential of astrophysical objects or condense into self-gravitating configurations. When these systems collapse in a bosenova, part of their mass is turned into relativistic radiation that escapes the galaxy. We bound the mass that a single object can eject and sum it over realistic models of the Milky Way and of other types of galaxies. For gravitational atoms, with realistic stellar populations and stellar evolution, the stars of the Milky Way deplete at most $ε^{\rm GA}_\star\simeq3\times10^{-9}$ of its halo, and the pump is equally negligible in other galaxies. The central black hole, Sgr A$^*$, could reach $ε^{\rm GA}\sim10^{-3}$, but only for a boson mass disfavoured by ultrafaint dwarf galaxies and beyond the validity of the perturbative treatment, where only a geometric bound on the dark matter flux is available. For boson stars feeding on the rest of the halo, these would radiate at most $\sim3\times10^{-5}$ of the Milky-Way halo and $0.1\%$ of a DF2-like one.

title: A Step-Like Transition Underlying the Life and Death of Galaxies
abstract: How galaxies stop forming stars is a complex and central problem in astrophysics. Numerous physical mechanisms have been proposed, yet a simple, unified framework connecting these mechanisms remains lacking. Here, we derive a step-function quenching response from the fundamental principle of gas mass conservation, governed by the competition between gas-supply and gas-depletion timescales. This response also enables the gas-supply timescale to be inferred from the observed quenched fraction. Applying this method to approximately 350,000 galaxies, we find a characteristic gas-supply timescale of ~1 Gyr, reveal distinct inside-out and outside-in quenching signatures associated with supermassive black holes and dark matter halos, respectively, and identify galaxies with intermediate stellar surface mass densities as occupying a critical state for quenching and rejuvenation. Our work establishes a unified physical framework in which a simple step-function response captures how diverse physical processes regulate galaxy quenching and the resumption of star formation through their effects on the competition between gas-supply and gas-depletion timescales.

title: A Parsec-Scale Transient High-Frequency-Peaked Radio Source in the Very Large Array Sky Survey Brightening and Fading over a Decadal Timescale
abstract: A subset of active galactic nuclei (AGN) manifests as compact radio sources with peaked radio spectra, commonly referred to as peaked-spectrum (PS) sources. Generally, PS sources are interpreted as young radio jets, but the early evolution of the jet is rarely observed and not fully understood. Here, we present VT J182357-234511 (VT J1823-2345), a radio transient in the Very Large Array Sky Survey (VLASS) that resembles a PS source. Notable properties of VT J1823-2345 include: (i) brightening by a factor of 3 between 1996 and 2021 at 1.4 GHz, (ii) peaked spectra with high frequency peaks at $ν_{\mathrm{p,obs}}\gtrsim6\,\mathrm{GHz}$, (iii) a peaked 3 GHz light curve that has been fading since 2023, (iv) a resolved Gaussian (major-axis) size of 0.4 mas in 2024, and (v) a linear polarization fraction $p_{\mathrm{L}}\simeq0.73\%$ at 8.8 GHz with an extreme Faraday rotation measure $\mathrm{RM_{\mathrm{obs}}} \sim +12,000\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$. On the sky, VT J1823-2345 coincides with a supernova remnant and an F-type star, but no background galaxy is seen. Based on the multi-wavelength properties, we disfavor Galactic transients, explosive extragalactic transients, and blazar variability as plausible explanations. We argue that VT J1823-2345 is consistent with a "short-lived" parsec-scale PS source with a decades-old jet that does not grow into a large-scale radio galaxy. From comparing the full VLASS light curves, we speculate that VT J1823-2345 is similar to many VLASS nuclear transients reported in the literature, which may represent an emerging class of transient radio jets, perhaps related to episodic AGN activity or jetted tidal disruption events.
